title: Cloud Deployment and Serving at Scale
summary: Move beyond running a container on your laptop and learn how to deploy a model to the cloud so it stays available, scales automatically, and rolls out safely. We cover managed ML endpoints, Kubernetes fundamentals for multi-replica serving, purpose-built serving runtimes like KServe and Triton, and how to choose between managed and self-managed approaches.
objectives: Explain why a single local container cannot meet production availability, autoscaling, and rollout needs
Push a container image to a registry and deploy it to a managed ML endpoint (SageMaker, Vertex AI, or Azure ML)
Describe the core Kubernetes objects for serving: pods, Deployments, Services, and horizontal autoscaling
Compare purpose-built serving runtimes (KServe, BentoML, Ray Serve, Triton) and what they add over a hand-rolled API
Connect a model registry to deployment by pulling and serving an approved model version
Choose between a managed endpoint and self-managed Kubernetes based on cost, control, and operational burden

quiz.q: Why is running `docker run` on your laptop inadequate for a production model service?
options: Docker images are always too large to transfer over the network
Laptops are physically unable to execute Python code
A single machine offers no high availability, no autoscaling, and only manual, risky rollouts
Containers cannot expose network ports outside the host
quiz.why: One laptop is a single point of failure with fixed capacity. Production needs redundancy across machines, automatic scaling under load, and controlled rollouts — none of which a lone `docker run` provides.

quiz.q: What is typically the first step when deploying a container image to a managed cloud ML service?
options: Push the built image to a container registry the service can pull from
Email the image file to the cloud provider's support team
Rewrite the model in the provider's proprietary serving language
Delete Docker and upload the raw Python source files instead
quiz.why: Managed services deploy from an image stored in a registry such as Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, or Azure Container Registry. You push once, then point the endpoint at the image tag.

quiz.q: In Kubernetes, which object manages a desired number of identical pod replicas and recreates them if they fail?
options: A ConfigMap
A Service
An Ingress
A Deployment
quiz.why: A Deployment declares the desired replica count and pod template; its controller continuously reconciles reality to that desired state, replacing crashed pods and enabling rolling updates.

quiz.q: What do purpose-built serving runtimes like KServe, BentoML, Ray Serve, and Triton add over a hand-rolled FastAPI app?
options: Nothing useful; they are strictly slower than FastAPI in every case
Built-in capabilities such as autoscaling, request batching, multi-model serving, and GPU optimization
They remove the need to containerize the model at all
They only work for image-classification models and nothing else
quiz.why: These runtimes bake in concerns you would otherwise build by hand: dynamic batching, scale-to-zero/autoscaling, hosting many models per server, and efficient GPU utilization.

quiz.q: What is NVIDIA Triton Inference Server primarily optimized for?
options: Packaging Python applications into pip wheels for distribution
Provisioning and managing the underlying Kubernetes cluster nodes
High-throughput GPU inference with dynamic batching across multiple frameworks
Training large models from scratch on distributed clusters
quiz.why: Triton is an inference server focused on maximizing GPU throughput — it supports dynamic batching and concurrent model execution across backends like TensorRT, PyTorch, and ONNX. It does not train models.

quiz.q: When would you choose a fully managed endpoint (SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML) over self-managing Kubernetes yourself?
quiz.answer: When you want lower operational burden — the provider handles infrastructure, scaling, patching, and uptime — and you are willing to trade some control and flexibility (and often higher per-hour cost) for speed and simplicity.
quiz.why: Managed endpoints minimize ops work and are ideal for small teams or when time-to-production matters; self-managed Kubernetes offers more control and potentially lower cost at scale but requires real platform expertise.

body_markdown:
## From `docker run` on Your Laptop to the Cloud

Earlier you containerized a model. Running `docker run -p 8000:8000 my-model` proves the image works — but it is not production. A single container on one machine has three fatal gaps:

- **No high availability:** if the process crashes or the machine reboots, the service is simply down.
- **No autoscaling:** fixed capacity means spikes cause timeouts while idle periods waste money.
- **No safe rollout:** shipping a new version means stopping the old one, with no gradual rollout or rollback.

The cloud solves these by running **many replicas across many machines**, behind a load balancer, managed by a control plane that restarts failures and scales on demand.

## Step 1: Push to a Registry, Run on a Managed Service

Cloud services deploy from an **image in a container registry**, not from your local Docker daemon. The flow is: build, tag, push, then point a managed endpoint at the image.

```bash
# Tag and push to a registry (Amazon ECR shown; GCP Artifact Registry / Azure ACR are analogous)
docker build -t my-model:1.0 .
docker tag my-model:1.0 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:1.0
docker push 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:1.0
```

Managed ML endpoints then take that image and run it for you with autoscaling, health checks, and HTTPS built in. The big-three options:

- **AWS SageMaker** — real-time and serverless inference endpoints.
- **Google Cloud Vertex AI** — online prediction endpoints from a custom container.
- **Azure Machine Learning** — managed online endpoints.

They differ in API, but the mental model is identical: *registry image in, scalable HTTPS endpoint out.*

## Kubernetes Basics for ML Serving

When you need more control than a managed endpoint, **Kubernetes (K8s)** is the standard. Four objects matter for serving:

- **Pod** — the smallest unit; one or more containers sharing a network namespace.
- **Deployment** — declares *how many* identical replicas you want and keeps them running, enabling rolling updates and rollback.
- **Service** — a stable DNS name that load-balances traffic across the pods.
- **HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA)** — adds or removes replicas based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics.

A minimal Deployment plus Service for our model:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-model
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-model
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-model
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: server
          image: 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-model
spec:
  selector:
    app: my-model
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8000
```

With `replicas: 3` you immediately get redundancy and load spreading — the core reason to use K8s for multi-replica serving.

## Horizontal Autoscaling

Fixed replicas still waste money or fall over under load. An HPA scales the Deployment automatically:

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: my-model
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-model
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
```

Now Kubernetes keeps average CPU near 70%, scaling between 2 and 10 pods as traffic changes.

## Purpose-Built Serving Runtimes

Hand-rolling FastAPI is fine for one model, but production serving has recurring needs. **Purpose-built runtimes** provide them out of the box:

- **KServe** — Kubernetes-native model serving with autoscaling (including scale-to-zero), canary rollout, and a standard inference protocol.
- **BentoML** — focuses on packaging and serving: bundle model, code, and dependencies into a deployable artifact with adaptive batching.
- **Ray Serve** — scalable Python-first serving; compose multiple models and scale across a Ray cluster.
- **NVIDIA Triton** — high-throughput GPU inference with **dynamic batching** and concurrent models across TensorRT, PyTorch, and ONNX backends.

The common wins over a bare API are **continuous/dynamic batching** (grouping concurrent requests to use the GPU efficiently), **multi-model hosting**, and **GPU-aware autoscaling** — work you would otherwise build yourself.

## From Model Registry to Deployment

A **model registry** (MLflow Registry, SageMaker Model Registry, Vertex Model Registry) is the handoff point between training and serving. Training produces and registers versions; deployment pulls the **approved** version and serves it.

```python
import mlflow

# Pull the version currently promoted to Production, not a hardcoded path
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/fraud-detector@champion")
prediction = model.predict(features)
```

This decouples *what* is deployed from *how*: the serving config references a version alias, so promoting a new model is a registry action and the same image serves whichever version the registry points to.

## Choosing an Approach

There is no single right answer — it is a trade-off:

- **Managed endpoint (SageMaker / Vertex AI / Azure ML):** lowest operational burden; the provider handles infra, scaling, and patching. Best for small teams and fast time-to-production. Trade-offs: less control and often higher per-hour cost.
- **Self-managed Kubernetes (+ KServe/Triton):** maximum control and flexibility, portable across clouds, potentially cheaper at large scale. Trade-off: you own the platform and need real K8s expertise.

Start managed when you can; reach for Kubernetes when scale, cost, custom hardware, or portability demands it.

slides.title: Kubernetes Building Blocks
bullets: Pod: smallest unit, runs your container
Deployment: keeps N identical replicas running
Service: stable address that load-balances pods
HPA: scales replicas on CPU or custom metrics
slides.narration: When you need more control than a managed endpoint, Kubernetes is the standard. A pod runs your container. A Deployment declares how many identical replicas you want and keeps them healthy, enabling rolling updates. A Service gives a stable address that load-balances across pods. And a HorizontalPodAutoscaler adds or removes replicas based on load.

slides.title: A Minimal Deployment
bullets: apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment
replicas: 3 gives redundancy and load spreading
Pod template points at your registry image
Controller recreates pods that crash
slides.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-model
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: my-model }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: my-model }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: server
          image: my-model:1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
slides.narration: Here is a minimal Deployment. apiVersion apps slash v1, kind Deployment, three replicas, and a pod template that runs your registry image on port 8000. With replicas set to three you immediately get redundancy and load spreading, and the controller recreates any pod that crashes. That is the core reason to use Kubernetes for multi-replica serving.

slides.title: Autoscaling with an HPA
bullets: Fixed replicas waste money or fall over
HPA targets a metric like 70% CPU
minReplicas / maxReplicas bound the range
Kubernetes adds or removes pods automatically
slides.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    kind: Deployment
    name: my-model
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
slides.narration: Fixed replica counts still waste money or fall over under load. A HorizontalPodAutoscaler fixes that by targeting a metric, here 70 percent average CPU, and scaling the Deployment between a minimum and maximum number of pods. Kubernetes then adds replicas under load and removes them when traffic drops, keeping utilization steady.

slides.title: Purpose-Built Serving Runtimes
bullets: KServe: Kubernetes-native serving, scale-to-zero
BentoML: packaging plus adaptive batching
Ray Serve: scalable Python-first serving

slides.narration: Hand-rolling FastAPI works for one model, but production serving has recurring needs. KServe is Kubernetes-native with autoscaling and canary rollout. BentoML focuses on packaging plus adaptive batching. Ray Serve scales Python serving across a cluster. And NVIDIA Triton maximizes GPU throughput with dynamic batching across frameworks. The common wins are batching, multi-model hosting, and GPU-aware autoscaling you'd otherwise build yourself.

slides.title: Registry Handoff and Choosing
bullets: Serving pulls the approved model version from the registry
Promote a model with a registry action, not a redeploy
Managed endpoint: least ops, less control, higher cost
Self-managed K8s: more control and cheaper at scale
slides.code:
import mlflow
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(
    "models:/fraud-detector@champion")

slides.narration: The model registry is the handoff between training and serving: deployment pulls the approved version by alias, so promoting a new model is a registry action rather than a code change. Finally, choosing an approach is a trade-off. Managed endpoints minimize operations but cost more and give less control. Self-managed Kubernetes offers control and lower cost at scale but demands real platform expertise. Start managed when you can.
